content.title: About
content.content: Edamame are young soybeans harvested before they fully mature and are usually served boiled or steamed in the pod. They have a mild, slightly sweet flavor and a pleasantly firm texture. Edamame are commonly eaten as a snack, added to salads, soups, and various Asian dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Edamame are a staple snack in Japan, China, and Korea, often served in bars and restaurants.
The soybeans used for edamame provide about 11 g of protein per 100 g of product.
In Japan they are traditionally sprinkled with sea salt, but they can also be flavored with spices, soy sauce, or garlic butter.
The Japanese name “edamame” (枝豆) means “beans on a branch.”
Edamame can be green or yellow depending on the soybean variety.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Edamame contain a complete set of essential amino acids, making them a valuable plant‑based protein source.

items.title: Good source of fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber supports digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Especially vitamin B6 and folate, which are important for metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Edamame provide polyunsaturated fatty acids, including omega‑3s, that support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Mineral content
items.content: They supply iron, magnesium, potassium, and calcium, essential for bones and muscles.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: People allergic to soy may experience reactions ranging from mild to severe anaphylaxis.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce the absorption of certain minerals; moderate consumption is advised.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: High purine levels may be problematic for individuals with gout.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Edamame are typically served in the pod: bite the beans out and discard the pod. They can be enjoyed hot or cold, seasoned with salt, spices, or soy sauce. The beans also work well in salads, rice dishes, pasta, or as a puree.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked edamame in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Raw frozen beans keep for up to 6 months in the freezer.
